question: What note-taking apps work offline and store notes as local Markdown files? Compare the main options.
answer:
ChatGPT 说：

If your requirements are:

Works fully offline
Stores notes as local Markdown (.md) files
Keeps your data usable outside the app

then the field narrows quite a bit. The main contenders are Obsidian, Logseq, Joplin, Zettlr, Typora, and iA Writer. 
N
Noteline
+1

Quick comparison
App	Local Markdown files	Offline	Best for	Main downside
Obsidian	✅ Yes, folders of .md files	✅ Yes	Personal knowledge base, "second brain"	Can become complex; official sync costs extra
Logseq	✅ Yes (.md or Org files)	✅ Yes	Daily notes, outlining, connected thinking	Bullet/block workflow is opinionated
Joplin	⚠️ Markdown-based, but managed in an app database	✅ Yes	Evernote replacement, privacy, clipping	Less "plain folder of Markdown" feeling
Zettlr	✅ Yes	✅ Yes	Research, academic writing, citations	Less ideal for casual notes
Typora	✅ Yes	✅ Yes	Clean Markdown writing	Not a knowledge-management system
iA Writer	✅ Yes	✅ Yes	Distraction-free writing	Limited linking/knowledge features
N
Noteline
+1
1. Obsidian — best general-purpose choice

Storage model: A folder called a "vault" containing ordinary Markdown files.

Strengths

Your notes are just .md files you can open anywhere.
Excellent backlinks: [[Note Name]].
Huge plugin ecosystem.
Good search, tags, graph view, canvases, templates.
Works well with Git, Syncthing, Dropbox, iCloud, etc. for DIY syncing. 
R
recal
+1

Weaknesses

Easy to spend more time configuring than writing.
Some features use Obsidian-specific Markdown extensions.
Official sync is a paid service. 
R
recal

Best for:
People building a long-lived personal knowledge base.

2. Logseq — best for outlining and daily journals

Storage model: Local Markdown or Org-mode files.

Strengths

Very strong daily notes workflow.
Everything is a block, so individual thoughts can be linked and referenced.
Open source.
Excellent for research notes, journaling, and Zettelkasten-style workflows. 
R
recal

Weaknesses

The "everything is a bullet" model does not suit everyone.
Long-form writing can feel awkward.
Some features depend on Logseq-specific conventions.

Best for:
People who naturally think in lists, fragments, and connected ideas.

3. Joplin — best traditional notes app with Markdown

Storage model: Markdown content stored locally, managed through Joplin's database structure.

Strengths

Open source.
Familiar notebook/folder model.
Strong import tools (including Evernote migration).
Web clipper.
Built-in encrypted sync options. 
A
AI:PRODUCTIVITY
+1

Weaknesses

Less transparent than "a folder full of Markdown files."
Linking and knowledge graphs are weaker than Obsidian/Logseq.

Best for:
People who want a classic notes app rather than a knowledge graph.

4. Zettlr — best for researchers and writers

Storage model: Plain Markdown files.

Strengths

Excellent Markdown support.
Designed around academic workflows.
Citation support.
Pandoc-based exports for PDF, Word, and LaTeX workflows. 
N
Noteline

Weaknesses

More specialized.
Less convenient for quick everyday capture.
No strong mobile ecosystem.

Best for:
Students, researchers, and people writing long documents.

5. Typora — best Markdown editor

Storage model: Normal Markdown files.

Strengths

Beautiful live Markdown preview.
Very pleasant writing experience.
Minimal distractions.
Great for people who already organize files themselves.

Weaknesses

Not really a note database.
No backlinks, graph, or knowledge-management features.

Best for:
"Give me a great Markdown editor, not a second brain."

6. iA Writer — best pure writing environment

Storage model: Markdown/text files.

Strengths

Excellent typography.
Focus mode.
Very polished.
Good for essays, drafts, and professional writing.

Weaknesses

Less flexible as a knowledge archive.
Paid app.

Best for:
Writers who value the act of writing more than organizing information.

My recommendations by use case
You want your notes to survive decades
Obsidian
Logseq
Zettlr

Plain Markdown folders are the most future-proof approach. 
R
recal

You want a "second brain"
Pick Obsidian.
You want daily journaling and idea capture
Pick Logseq.
You want an Evernote replacement
Pick Joplin.
You write papers, books, or technical documents
Pick Zettlr.
You only want a beautiful Markdown editor
Pick Typora or iA Writer.

For most people who specifically say "offline + local Markdown files," I would start with Obsidian, because it gives you the simplest long-term storage model with the most room to grow.
